lesson.title: P→F Discrimination Drills
lesson.subtitle: Which f-words are true p-shifts — and which are ancient f impostors?

hook.title: The F Police
hook.content: Not every German f descends from an English p. Most do — hoffen, helfen, Schiff, Affe, reif — but German also has honest, ancient f-words that were never anything else: Flug (flight) and fressen. The skill you build today is the customs check: when you meet a German f-word, ask whether trading its f for a p produces an English word. hoffen → hope? Stamp it through. Flug → 'plug'? No — Flug is native Germanic f, kin to fly and flight, which also start with f.

footnotes.title: Two F's, Two Ages
footnotes.content: Proto-Germanic already owned an f (from an even older PIE p — Grimm's Law, thousands of years before the High German Shift). fly/flight/Flug carry that ancient f. The High German Shift (500–700 AD) is a second, younger wave that turned remaining p's into f's and pf's.

pattern.title: The Customs Check: Swap f for p
pattern.content: Run the swap test: hoffen → hoppen? hope! helfen → help! schlafen — the schl- cluster hides 'sleep' with p → f: sleep → schlafen. Schiff → skipper's Schiff: ship (and a ship-master is still a skipper in English). Affe → ape. reif → ripe. scharf → sharp. greifen → grip. Now the impostors: Flug (fly/flight), frei (free), Fisch (fish), Feuer (fire) — no p hides inside these; their f is the ancient Germanic one English shares. Impostors are cognates too — just not students of this shift.
pattern.linguist_note: The swap test has a third outcome: stumpf (stump/blunt) shows final p → pf, and treffen pairs the P→F shift with D → T (English dræpan, 'to strike' — the same root as drape). Mixed-shift words are the exception, not the rule.

exercises.prompt: Pass the customs check — match each German f-word to its English p-twin:
exercises.target_answer: hoffen, helfen, scharf, greifen, Pflanze, Pfirsich
exercises.meaning: to hope, to help, sharp, to grip, plant, peach
exercises.explanation: Swapping f for p exposes the English twin hiding in each German word — and Pflanze does the double shift: p → pf up front, t → z at the back.

exercises.prompt: German 'Flug' (flight) — is its f a product of the P → F shift?
options: Flug has no English cognate at all
Yes — but only in northern Germany
Yes — Flug is 'plug' with the p shifted
No — Flug is an ancient f-word, kin to English fly and flight
exercises.target_answer: No — Flug is an ancient f-word, kin to English fly and flight
exercises.meaning: Not every f is a shifted p — some f's are ancestral
exercises.explanation: Flug and flight share the older Germanic f. The p → f shift is a younger wave; it only hit words that still had a p.

exercises.prompt: Which German word is the true p-shift twin of English 'sleep'?
exercises.explanation: sleep → schlafen: the sl- cluster became schl- and p became f. The other three verbs have no p inside.

exercises.prompt: Swap the f back: what English verb is the twin of 'treffen' (to meet/strike)?
exercises.explanation: treffen is a double-shift word: English dræpan 'to strike' → d → t and p → ff. Modern English kept the root in drape.

exercises.idea: it's late and your friend is still up, so you tell her: I hope you sleep
cues: Who hopes? → ich hoffe (your P → FF verb, working ending and all)
Who sleeps? → du schläfst — schlaf- + the thou-ending -st
Sleep is the p-shift word: English sleep → schlafen, here in its du form

vocab_hints.note: stem schlaf- + the Shakespearean -st (thou sleepest); the ä is the du-vowel change

exercises.explanation: 'Ich hoffe' + 'du schläfst' — the p-shift verb takes the ancient thou-ending: thou sleepest → du schläfst.

summary.outcome: Sort German f-words into true p-shifts and ancestral f cognates on sight.
summary.takeaway: Swap f for p: if an English word appears, it is the P→F shift at work; if not, the f is an honest ancient one.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the dental hardening up close — thunder-day, bath towns, and why du is really thou.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from P→F Discrimination Drills (I hope you sleep):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich hoffe du schläfst" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of P→F Discrimination Drills without relying on short-term echo.

helfen.etymology_derivation: p → f. Governs the dative case (mir).

schlafen.etymology_derivation: p → f with sl- → schl- cluster.

schiff.etymology_derivation: P → FF shift. Cognate with English "ship" and living nautical twin "skipper" (literally Schiff-er, ship-master).

greifen.context_translation: He grasps / grips for my hand.

treffen.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and p → ff (cognate with English "drap" / strike).

pflanze.shift_rule: P → PF / F + T → S / SS / Z
pflanze.etymology_derivation: Double shift: initial p → pf and t → z [ts].

pfirsich.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic persik, from Late Latin persicum, meaning Persian apple; English peach descends from the same Latin word, with p corresponding to German pf. [wiktionary]

irgendwo.context_phrase: Mein Handy ist irgendwo im Haus.
irgendwo.context_translation: My phone is somewhere in the house.
irgendwo.etymology_derivation: Irgend (any, at all) plus wo (where, the twin of English where); literally anywhere, that is somewhere. [wiktionary]

geschäft.context_phrase: Das Geschäft öffnet um neun Uhr.
geschäft.context_translation: The shop opens at nine o'clock.
geschäft.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *gaskafti, a doing of the schaffen (to make) family — the root whose English twin is shape, as the schaffen page lists. [wiktionary]

pflaster.context_phrase: Ich klebe ein Pflaster auf die Wunde.
pflaster.context_translation: I stick a plaster on the wound.
pflaster.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin plastrum via Proto-West Germanic *plastr and Old High German pflastar — the p became pf in German, while English plaster kept p, borrowed from the same Latin source. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
